newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia bonds see puny kick-off to 1997.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia bonds see puny kick-off to 1997.

text.p: *Australian bond yields ended the first trading day of the year higher reflecting weakness in U.S. Treasuries prior to the New Year holiday, but turnover was fairly feeble.
*Immediate local focus on today's December U.S. NAPM index.

The Australian bond market failed to break out of the holiday torpor with several centres staying closed within the Asia region, although yields were higher reflecting weakness in the U.S. prior to the New Year holiday.

The resumption of bond trading on the Sydney Futures Exchange, rather than through the screen based SYCOM system, failed to enliven a market which remains transfixed by developments offshore in the near-term.
The immediate focus is on the U.S. December National Association of Purchasing Management index later today, which is forecast to ease to 52.3 from 52.7 in November.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics released its latest report on business expectations, which saw profits falling 2.9 percent in the March quarter from the previous quarter and was the smallest decrease recorded for a March quarter.

The bureau also found businesses expected sales to rise 0.4 percent in the March quarter, the first time the survey has recorded a rise in expectations for the first quarter, while capital expenditure was expected to increase 5.8 percent, the biggest expected lift in 12 months.
However, the data failed to stir the market into action with Monday's balance of payments seen as the next major local event.

"...the (business) survey responses would have been made prior to the third rate cut. It is probably best to regard these expectations as reflecting the state of the economy that led to the rate cuts," said Chris Caton, chief econmist at Bankers Trust Australia in a report.
The Reserve Bank cut official interest rates three times in 1996, the last being to 6.0 percent on December 11.

The local market was marked down sharply at the start of trading following a steep sell-off in U.S. Treasuries on Tuesday on data showing strong growth in November housing starts and a rise in December consumer confidence.

The local market saw resistance in pushing the 10-year bond yield through 7.50 percent at the opening, causing yield spreads to the U.S. and Canada to tighten. The yield curve steepened slightly with the long end feeling a greater impact from the U.S. bond fall. Both Japan and New Zealand were closed today.
